items.title: Derrick Gardner interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 9, 2013
items.q: You know like Kenny Dorham did that with “All the Things You Are.” He wrote — well now I can’t think of the name of the tune

ctx.x: Well it kind of brings me to a question and I’m not sure how to ask it. But does music for you, or especially in your own compositions, does it have to mean something? Does it have to have a subtext or can it just be music?

I think that there is music that can be written to be functional, you know, that serves a purpose. Like I was just talking to Doc Woods about this earlier today. He was talking about writing for films. And the music has to convey a mood and not take away from the dialogue that’s being conveyed in the film. Or background music at a restaurant, you know, it serves a purpose. But when you’re composing music to be really listened to, concertized music, or even when you’re improvising, I’m one that believes that you…

I had to chuckle because I read a quote of yours and it was almost exactly a quote that I got from Ed Shaughnessy years ago, and it was about if you look out there and at least some of the people aren’t moving or tapping your feet, you’re not doing your job.
